name: Daria Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Daria, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Does that sound all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine. I'll be honest with you, though some of it might sound old-fashioned.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Hartley & Owusu, a small practice in the town where I grew up, six of us in an old house by the church. I do accounts and tax returns for family businesses: a funeral home, two garages, a farm shop, and the parish accounts every spring. I do everything in the software we've had for ten years and on paper files, and I've never used any of the AI tools; I don't trust them with clients' figures. Mrs Hartley, the senior partner, still reviews nearly everything I do, because I'm slow and I miss the odd adjustment. What I love is that clients ask for me by name at the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. I'd be glad of that, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, these things always get oversold. I'd say it at church and at work, not online, I'm hardly online at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. Our clients are family businesses who want a person they know, and Mrs Hartley isn't buying anything clever. My job carries on as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep working towards my exams, slowly. Marco and I would go ahead with the wedding next June as planned, about fourteen thousand, mostly saved already. I'd keep doing his plumbing business's books in the evenings for free, like I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a good day at work look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the funeral home's owner, Mr Albright, brings his receipts in a biscuit tin and we go through them together over tea. It takes twice as long as it should. But he trusts me. Clients ask for me by name at the door, and that matters more to me than being quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything outside AI worrying you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Marco's business is busy, we've got the house with help from both families, and we've saved more than enough. My mum's knee is bad, so I help her on Saturdays, but that's family, not a worry.

say: I'd say I'm **not surprised**, because these things always get oversold.
I'd say it at **church** and at work, but hardly ever online.
think: I'd be **relieved**, because family businesses want a **person they know**.
The senior partner isn't buying anything **clever**, so my job carries on.
do: Hold the **wedding** next June, about fourteen thousand, mostly saved.
Keep doing my fiancé's **plumbing books** for free in the evenings.
S0.quote: Clients ask for me by name at the door, and that matters more to me than being quick.
fieldNote: Her **work** and **money** feel secure: savings, a house and a busy fiancé.
She values **trust** over speed, and her small firm shares that view.
Her resistance to AI is rooted in **client confidentiality** as much as habit.

steps.text: Keep doing family business accounts by hand at the small practice
Hold the fourteen-thousand wedding next June as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I suppose that's closer to what the papers say will happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small firms like ours will be fine because people still want someone they trust, and I'd mean it. I'd say businesses should be free to choose, but nobody should be forced onto software they don't want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm not sure. The big online firms would offer tax returns for half our price, and some of our younger clients would go. If my small firm loses a fifth of its clients, they won't need two juniors, and I'm the slower one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep the clients who like me close, the funeral home, the farm shop. I'd wait a year to see whether our clients actually leave before doing anything drastic. I'd keep the wedding but put an extra two hundred a month into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I don't like the idea of being pushed into things I don't trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the AI tools if Mrs Hartley asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If she asked, yes, because she's the boss and she's been good to me. But I'd check every figure by hand. I'd be slower than ever for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if your job went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not Mrs Hartley. The big firms that undercut everyone, and the tech companies that sell to them. And maybe people who'd rather save fifty pounds than know who's doing their tax.

say: I'd say small firms survive because people want **someone they trust**.
I'd say businesses should **choose freely**, not be forced onto software.
think: Big online firms could **undercut** us by **half**.
If we lose a fifth of clients, the **slower junior** goes, and that's me.
do: Keep **loyal clients** like the funeral home and farm shop close.
**Wait a year** to see if clients actually leave.
Add **two hundred** a month to savings and keep the wedding.
feel: **Anxious** about being **pushed** into things I don't trust.
S1.quote: If my small firm loses a fifth of its clients, they won't need two juniors, and I'm the slower one.
fieldNote: She sees **price competition** from big online firms as the real threat.
She blames **big firms** and tech companies, never her own boss.
She'd adopt AI **only if told**, and would double-check everything.

steps.text: Keep loyal clients like the funeral home close with personal service
Wait a year to see whether clients move to online firms
Add two hundred a month to savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's not a change, that's an ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong and it's moving too fast, and that families and churches will have to look after each other. I wouldn't ask for handouts, but I'd say the companies doing this should answer for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job's gone, maybe by the end of 2028. The paperwork side of Marco's business goes too, but his actual plumbing has about three more years before the robots. So the family income would be his hands, for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the practice when it shrinks and work in Marco's business full-time, doing his books, booking jobs and answering the phone, and maybe learning to do simple jobs with him. We'd make the wedding small, at the church hall, and put the rest towards the business. I'd lean on my parents for things like childcare later, if we had a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd pray about it a lot, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the wedding look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Church in the morning, sandwiches in the hall, my aunt doing the cake. About four thousand instead of fourteen. My mother would be upset for a week and then say it was lovely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd answer Marco's phones. Couldn't AI do that too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, and quicker. But my fiancé's customers are old ladies with leaking boilers who want to hear a person on the phone. I'd hold on to that for as long as it lasts.

say: I'd say it's wrong and too fast, and families must **look after each other**.
I'd want the **companies** responsible to answer for it, not ask for handouts.
think: My job is likely **gone** by the end of **2028**.
My fiancé's **plumbing** has about **three years** before the robots.
do: Join my fiancé's **plumbing business** full-time doing books and bookings.
Shrink the **wedding** to about **four thousand** at the church hall.
Lean on my **parents** for help later if we have children.
S2.quote: My fiancé's customers are old ladies with leaking boilers who want to hear a person on the phone.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** and relies on her fiancé's **hands-on** trade.
She rejects **handouts**, turning to family and church instead.
Faith is part of how she copes: she'd **pray** about it.

steps.text: Work full-time in her fiancé's plumbing business doing books and bookings
Cut the wedding to four thousand at the church hall
Ask her parents to help with childcare later

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is still quick, but at least I'd see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot of change and families will need to stick together. I'd say we need more apprenticeships, real ones, so young people can learn trades while there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd lose the job, just later, probably around 2030 when the practice shrinks. Marco's plumbing would be safe until about 2034, so we'd have a bit of time to set ourselves up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job while it lasts and have the wedding as planned. I'd start doing more of Marco's business in the evenings now, so moving across is easy. We'd try for children sooner, maybe 2027, while we both have income and my parents are fit enough to help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less frightened, more watchful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why have children sooner rather than later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because later might be worse, not better. And my mum would be over the moon. I'd rather have a baby while there's money coming in than wait for a calm that never comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go back to studying anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'm not one for courses. I'd learn on the job from Marco, the way his dad taught him.

say: I'd say families will need to **stick together** through the change.
I'd call for **real apprenticeships** so young people learn trades in time.
think: I'd lose the job around **2030**, when the practice shrinks.
My fiancé's plumbing is safe until about **2034**.
do: Do more of my fiancé's **business admin** in the evenings now.
Have the **wedding** as planned next June.
S3.quote: I'd rather have a baby while there's money coming in than wait for a calm that never comes.
fieldNote: She still expects to **lose her job**, but the household keeps the fiancé's income.
Five years makes her **bring children forward**, a striking choice.
She'd learn **on the job** from family, not through courses.

steps.text: Take on more of her fiancé's business admin in the evenings
Try for a first child around 2027
Keep the job at the practice while it lasts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time. I'd have children at school by then, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for families to prepare, and they should. I'd say the government shouldn't try to run it all; firms and families should sort it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have most of my working years as an accountant before it ends. Then Marco's trade carries us until about 2039. I'd be thirty-seven and probably running his office by then anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job, finish my exams eventually, and have the wedding as planned. We'd put money into Marco's business, maybe a second van and an apprentice, about twenty thousand over a few years. I'd keep the AI out of my work as long as Mrs Hartley lets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's far enough off that I'd mostly get on with life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd keep AI out of your work. For how long, realistically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Until someone makes me, probably. Mrs Hartley retires around 2030 and whoever takes over will want it. Then I'd learn the minimum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future children about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn something with your hands, and look after your family, is what my grandfather said, and it seems truer now than ever.

say: I'd say ten years is enough for **families to prepare**.
I'd say the **government** shouldn't try to run it all.
think: I'd have **most** of my working years as an accountant first.
My fiancé's **trade** carries us until about **2039**.
do: Invest about **twenty thousand** in a second van and an **apprentice**.
Have the **wedding** as planned and finish exams eventually.
Keep **AI** out of my work until a new boss requires it.
S4.quote: Learn something with your hands, and look after your family, is what my grandfather said, and it seems truer now than ever.
fieldNote: She still expects her **accounting job** to end, so anxious despite feeling uneasy.
She bets the household on the fiancé's **trade** and an **apprentice**.
Her advice to future children echoes a **grandfather**, reflecting traditional values.

steps.text: Put about twenty thousand into a second van and an apprentice
Keep working at the practice without AI until required
Hold the wedding next June as planned

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years is too short for anyone to prepare, and I'd be leaning on Marco before we're even settled. What would help is real apprenticeships and help for small family businesses to take people on, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe faith. People like me will get through this through family and church, not through an app. Nobody in these conversations seems to count that.

headlineQuote: People like me will get through this through family and church, not through an app.
portrait: Daria is a **junior accountant** at a six-person practice in her hometown, serving family businesses and the parish.
She has **never used AI**, distrusts it with client figures, and values being asked for by name.
She has strong **savings**, a house and a fiancé who runs a **plumbing** business.
She moves from calm to **alarmed**, blaming big firms and tech companies, not her boss.
Her plan is to join her fiancé's **trade**, leaning on family and church.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028**, which leaves **no time** to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: Real **apprenticeships** and help for **family businesses** to hire, not handouts.
